Josh’s five-minute demo guide

One request.
One confirmed delivery.

An event rental order grows from 120 to 160 guests. Three employees use AI successfully. Show why the customer still needs one coordinated answer, then show the workflow that completes it.

The setup

Harbor Event Rentals serves Northstar’s Friday event. Rachel requests 40 more guests, with delivery still at 9 AM to the same venue. The order needs 40 extra chairs, 10 extra tables and a second truck. The additional charge is $580 before tax.

How to present it

Josh hosts and operates the demo. Suuchi explains the workflow change and handles the build discussion. Stay with one visible artifact at a time. Use the three employee tabs briefly, then follow the order through its decisions. Leave exceptions and implementation detail for Q&A.

0:00 - 0:40 · Scene 1Open scene 1

“Can we add 40 guests?”

Josh: Show Rachel’s request beside the original order. Point to 120 → 160 and the unchanged Friday, 9 AM delivery.

“You run an event rental company. A customer adds 40 guests. Same venue. Same Friday delivery. It sounds like one small request.”

“But the answer depends on the equipment, the trucks and the price agreeing. Let’s see what happens when everyone already has AI.”

This is a fictional rental company and illustrative order. The demo begins with a normal customer change, not an employee mistake.

0:40 - 1:45 · Scene 2Open scene 2

Three people use AI. Three useful answers.

Josh: Select Leah, Sam and Dana in turn. Show each short AI exchange and the result saved in that employee’s own system.

  1. Leah · Customer Service“Leah uses ChatGPT to understand the request and draft a reply. She records the change in HubSpot. The customer knows someone is handling it.”
  2. Sam · Warehouse“Sam uses Copilot with the rental inventory. He checks the equipment and saves a pending plan for 160 chairs and 40 tables. His part is correct.”
  3. Dana · Dispatch“Dana uses Claude to work through the delivery change. She reviews a second truck for the same 9 AM delivery and saves the dispatch plan. That adds $180.”

“Nobody forgot to update their system. Their AI helped them do their jobs. These answers are still in three separate places.”

A saved pending plan is not a released reservation or a confirmed delivery. The employees own their reviews. The AI does not invent stock availability or authorize a truck.

1:45 - 2:35 · Scene 3Open scene 3

The customer still needs one answer.

Josh: Show Leah’s draft. Explain the information she must bring together before she can make one complete commitment.

“Leah can draft a friendly response in seconds. But before she can confirm anything, she needs Sam’s equipment plan, Dana’s truck plan and the complete price.”

“The equipment adds $400. The second truck adds $180. Someone has to combine that, ask Rachel to approve the extra $580, and make sure the same version reaches the order and dispatch.”

“AI made each task easier. Leah is still coordinating the work.”

Do not claim a private AI session automatically knows every business system. The problem is the missing shared workflow, not the quality of Leah’s prompt. Do not attach fictional minutes or measured savings to the example.

2:35 - 4:20 · Scene 4Open scene 4

Same request. Connected work.

Josh: Run the connected example. Pause at the owner decisions, Rachel’s additional-charge approval and Leah’s final release. Show the saved-record checks.

  1. The request“The request and the saved source plans are attached to one order revision. We can see exactly which equipment, delivery and price commitments are changing.”
  2. Owner decisions“Sam approves the inventory plan. Dana approves the dispatch plan. Their decisions now belong to the same order, instead of separate conversations Leah has to reconcile.”
  3. Customer approval“The combined change is $580. Rachel approves that additional charge. The workflow cannot treat a draft message as customer consent.”
  4. Release and verify“Leah releases the approved revision. The workflow applies the agreed updates and checks the order, dispatch and CRM records. It only reports completion when they agree.”

Suuchi: “This is the part we build: connect the source records, move the decisions to the right owners, and carry the approved result into the systems. People still decide what the company can promise.”

Every approval and write in this prototype is simulated. Label Rachel’s response as a sample customer approval. Nothing is reserved, charged or sent to a real customer.

“Rachel gets one clear answer. The equipment, delivery and price match the approved order. Leah can review and send the confirmation.”

“We did not give these people another AI tool. We connected the work they were already doing.”

Suuchi: “Think of one request in your business that makes someone chase three systems. That is a good place to start.”

Josh: “Our complimentary workflow assessment is a separate session. Bring that request. We’ll map the handoffs and identify what it would take to complete the work.”

Q&A: what Nine-67 would build
  1. Authorized source connections. The customer request, CRM order, rental inventory and dispatch records, matched to the same order and source revision.
  2. A shared change record. Guest count, equipment quantities, delivery time, venue, charges and links to the reviewed evidence.
  3. Explicit decisions. Warehouse and dispatch reviews, customer approval of the extra charge, and a final release. Waiting, follow-up and escalation remain visible.
  4. Verified updates. Apply the approved revision, check the saved records, and report partial failures instead of presenting unfinished work as complete.

The workflow uses permitted business records and saved work products. It does not silently read private AI chats. Rental inventory and Dispatch board are fictional sample applications, not claims of live vendor integrations.

Q&A: why a shared chat is not the whole solution

A shared chat can make the discussion easier to find. The remaining work is recording which revision was approved, updating the equipment order and dispatch plan, and verifying that the customer-facing commitment matches those records. The demonstration makes those completion steps explicit.

If a required decision is missing or a write fails, the final confirmation must stay blocked. If the request changes again, approvals for an older version cannot be treated as approval of the new commitment.
